scenes.text: How could a promise that big fall so fast?

sentences.text: In January 1920, a man in Boston named Charles Ponzi started a firm called the Securities Exchange Company.
He promised clients a fifty percent profit within forty-five days.
In the first month, eighteen people invested a total of one thousand eight hundred dollars.
So how could a promise that big fall apart so fast?
sentences.editorial: central question, asked before the answer

scenes.label: in his pocket on arrival, by his own account

scenes.quote: I landed in this country with $2.50 in cash and $1 million in hopes, and those hopes never left me
scenes.speaker: Charles Ponzi

sentences.text: Ponzi was born in Lugo, in Italy.
On the fifteenth of November 1903, he arrived in Boston aboard the steamship Vancouver.
By his own account, he had two dollars and fifty cents in his pocket.
Later he said he landed with two dollars fifty in cash and a million dollars in hopes.

quote.text: I landed in this country with $2.50 in cash and $1 million in hopes, and those hopes never left me
quote.speaker: Charles Ponzi

scenes.label: taken in a day, late July 1920
coupons needed to cover the money

sentences.text: His story was that he bought international reply coupons cheaply abroad and redeemed them at face value in the United States.
Between February and March 1920, the money invested rose from five thousand to twenty-five thousand dollars.
By late July, Ponzi was taking in two hundred and fifty thousand dollars a day.
But to cover the money, a hundred and sixty million coupons would have had to exist, and only about twenty-seven thousand did.

scenes.text: The Boston Post starts asking questions

scenes.quote: I went looking for trouble, and I found it.
scenes.speaker: Charles Ponzi, to reporters, 1934

scenes.text: Would you have trusted fifty percent in forty-five days?

sentences.text: On the twenty-sixth of July 1920, the Boston Post started asking hard questions.
Investors lost about twenty million dollars in nineteen-twenty money.
Charged with eighty-six counts of mail fraud, Ponzi was sentenced to five years in federal prison.
Released in 1934, he told reporters that he went looking for trouble and found it.

quote.text: I went looking for trouble, and I found it.
quote.speaker: Charles Ponzi

sentences.text: He died in Rio de Janeiro in 1949, leaving an estate of seventy-five dollars.
Would you have trusted a promise of fifty percent in forty-five days?
